Snir Broshi said:

Normal programming languages don't have dependent types

Really? I think it's pretty common; for example, in Java (a mainstream programming language since the mid-90s), List<Cat> and List<Dog> would be incompatible types, one a list of Cat objects and the other a list of Dogs.

I believe that difference doesn't exist in the compiled bytecode, but it exists as far as the compiler is concerned.

Michael said:

Snir Broshi said:

Normal programming languages don't have dependent types

Really? I think it's pretty common; for example, in Java (a mainstream programming language since the mid-90s), List<Cat> and List<Dog> would be incompatible types, one a list of Cat objects and the other a list of Dogs.

I believe that difference doesn't exist in the compiled bytecode, but it exists as far as the compiler is concerned.

This is OOP, I think the dependent type theory is related to functional
That doesn't make any sense. It's part of the type system. The written style of your code is not a related concern.

For Rust, https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/types/parameters.html suggests that it also has parameterized types:

Here, first has type A, referring to to_vec's A type parameter; and rest has type Vec<A>, a vector with element type A.

Michael said:

That doesn't make any sense. It's part of the type system. The written style of your code is not a related concern.

What do you think dependent type theory is? Because just looking at the canonical sources, it is very much about functional programming. I have not heard anyone talk about classes in OOP interchangeably as a dependent type.
Rust also does not have dependent types natively afaik, but again its very much about definitions here.
This is exactly the same concept as how, in Lean, List Nat and List Int are different types.
I think dependent types are things like DihedralGroup 4 or List Int where you construct a type from arguments. Do you think differently?

As far as I know dependent type theory is defined via Pi and Sigma types, and the rest is inductive whistles and bells and etc. This is just the theory behind it. I am not sure defining dependent types as simply in any programming language, a type that is parameterised in some sense, is strong enough.

Michael said:

I think dependent types are things like DihedralGroup 4 or List Int where you construct a type from arguments. Do you think differently?

Parameterized types and dependent types are distinct concepts. List Int is not a dependent type in the usual usage of the word, because Int is a type, not a value.

Well, let's ask Theorem Proving in Lean 4:

2.8 What makes dependent type theory dependent?
The short explanation is that types can depend on parameters. You have already seen a nice example of this: the type List α depends on the argument α, and this dependence is what distinguishes List Nat and List Bool. For another example, consider the type Vector α n, the type of vectors of elements of α of length n. This type depends on two parameters: the type of the elements in the vector (α : Type) and the length of the vector n : Nat.

https://leanprover.github.io/theorem_proving_in_lean4/Dependent-Type-Theory/#what-makes-dependent-type-theory-dependent
That seems extremely explicit. Dependent types are types that depend on parameters. They are the same thing as parameterized types.
I assure you parametricity is rather distinct and orthogonal to the discussion as far as PL theory goes
Did you disagree with something I said, or something in the quote from TPIL? Or is this more of a "being right about all the facts won't make you right in spirit" thing?

I think this is an over-extension of the wording of an introductory text. If we took this at face value you'd have to conclude that something like System F has dependent types, which is simply not how this terminology is used.

Chris Henson said:

List Int is not a dependent type in the usual usage of the word, because Int is a type, not a value.

But Int is a value. It's a value of type Type. That's the whole point of the flowchart Snir posted.

You aren't really engaging with the things I am saying, and are playing semantics. I will spend some time gathering some sources for you perhaps, you might be surprised Lean violates certain parametricity whilst having dependent types.

Overall though, this boils down to definitions, and dependent types have a specific one.

Intuitively these concepts are similar, but for example not instantiating a type and having the compiler not complain, resolved at runtime, is something you might be accustomed to in other languages. And that is not a dependent type, but can be parametricity.

TPIL is not the place you will find PL theory considerations, thats more FPIL.

It's type theory; are there terms that aren't types?
Nat.zero?
(deleted)
Is that not a distinct type from the Nat.succ type family?
Well it's not a type, so I guess not.
Can you explain what you mean by "Nat.succ type family"? Nat.succ is a constructor of Nats, so not a type and not a family

Bear in mind you cannot form statements of the form "A = B" if they are not the same type. So you cannot even say "1 = 2" as a statement or really anything if they aren't the same type, it will be ill typed so it will give you an error immediately.

Snir Broshi said:

Can you explain what you mean by "Nat.succ type family"? Nat.succ is a constructor of Nats, so not a type and not a family

I'm calling Nat.succ a constructor of types in the same way that DihedralGroup is a constructor of types, where DihedralGroup 4 and DihedralGroup 5 are distinct types.

Yeah but notice that the type of DihedralGroup is Nat → Type, but the type of Nat.succ is Nat → Nat.
Hence one is called a type constructor, but the other isn't.

Eh it just constructs terms though, its the reason "x = 3" and "x = 5" are distinct types as propositions even. They depend on terms, which is the benefit of dependent types, depending on specific terms of a type.

Yan Yablonovskiy 🇺🇦 said:

Eh it just constructs terms though, its the reason "x = 3" and "x = 5" are distinct types as propositions even. They depend on terms, which is the benefit of dependent types, depending on specific terms of a type.

In the model where 3 and 5 are distinct subtypes of Nat, possessing just one term each, wouldn't the same benefit exist?
Then which one is x in/equal to? It has to be well typed so both sides have to be of the same type to even parse at all.

Michael said:

distinct subtypes of Nat

By "subtypes" do you mean Subtype?

Snir Broshi said:

By "subtypes" do you mean Subtype?

No, I mean something different; sorry.

Yan Yablonovskiy 🇺🇦 said:

Then which one is x in?

You're right that this would require an "equality" decider which is a function from α → β → Prop rather than being a function from α → α → Prop, but I don't see that as much of an obstacle.
If you have a relation between types that lets you compare them, that's what I was calling "subtypes".

I mean thats vaguely adjacent to how Prop works and prop_ext works, being able to say two Prop are equal that way. And there are other situations you have similar properties, but Nat has specific Peano axioms you should follow and things like injectivity of succ become real murky with whatever you are alluding to!
Also just FYI you certainly DO NOT NEED DEPENDENT TYPES to encode Nat, or even close, or even to do (almost the entirety of?) math, if thats the confusion!

Yan Yablonovskiy 🇺🇦 said:

Also just FYI you certainly DO NOT NEED DEPENDENT TYPES to encode Nat, or even close, or even to do (almost the entirety of?) math, if thats the confusion!

Don't worry; I definitely didn't mean to imply otherwise?

What I've said is that (many) normal programming languages have dependent types. They have a type system and it's frequent that dependent types are part of that type system. It's also frequent that the language's type system is more restrictive than is theoretically possible, but that doesn't stop dependent types from being dependent types.

things like injectivity of succ become real murky with whatever you are alluding to

I'm not sure I see what you're referring to, but I'd like to hear more about it. I have a vague belief that injectivity of succ comes from an axiom somewhere in Lean's type system, and that this axiom is related to the idea that the constructors of an inductive type are exhaustive.

It's not obvious to me why tightening the idea of which divisions of the numbers are "types" while loosening the idea of which can be compared to each other gets in the way of that assumption. Wouldn't you still have the same objects, being constructed in the same way, subject to the same axiom that there are no other ways?

No it was just we were embarking on a quest to get naturals to work seemingly without the dependent type aspect , so that’s why I said that, not because you said otherwise.

Type systems come in various shapes and forms , most languages esp in OOP are often rather fundamentally different in the strictness of typing and the concept of runtime errors (is a very different notion in Lean if it can even be defined appropriately).

A type in a system can “depend” on something , whatever it may be , in the English sense of the word. And then there are dependent types , which if a type system has or does not is not strictly about the meaning of the English word .

I should note that I think the assumed machinery of inductive types is what gives me the strong intuition that each constructor defines its own type.

In particular, I don't see a difference between inductive ThreeThings | a | b | c (assuming that syntax is correct) and a sum type composed from three "different" inductive types A, B, and C.

Michael said:

I should note that I think the assumed machinery of inductive types is what gives me the strong intuition that each constructor defines its own type.

In particular, I don't see a difference between inductive ThreeThings | a | b | c (assuming that syntax is correct) and a sum type composed from three "different" inductive types A, B, and C.

There are also indices and the inductive can indeed be its own type , but that’s slightly seperate. Indeed that is essentially the gist of what an inductive is , it also just comes with some prebuilt and bundled conveniences. You can use the recursive intro pattern matching on it as it was an Or, which is technically also inductive but can be thought of as basically the sum type for prop
If A, B, C each have one member, then yes, they're equivalent. A, B, C don't have to be different though, because a sum type is the disjoint union. Bool ⊕ Bool ⊕ Bool has 6 members.

Jeremy Chen said:

If A, B, C each have one member, then yes, they're equivalent.

But if this is the case, I don't see why there's supposed to be a typing difficulty with x = 3 and x = 5 when 3 and 5 are considered to inhabit their own highly specialized types. It's already the case that, by default, we can form x : ThreeThings = ThreeThings.a and x : ThreeThings = ThreeThings.c. Snir Broshi said:

I agree their List Nat example is strange, but

I think I can explain the structure of the section. The following example is cons, a function that prepends a value to a list. TPIL wants to explain that cons has a complicated type - it takes a value (with some arbitrary type), and a list (of elements of "that" type), and returns another list of elements of "that" type.

This is expressed as cons having type α : Type → a : α → List α → List α.

The point is that the type of the return value, List α, depends on the value α. But for this to make sense, α has to be a type. Types are values too.

So, for purposes of the whole section, there isn't a distinction between List Nat being parameterized on Nat, or Vector α n being parameterized on α, or Vector α n being parameterized on n. The dependent type List Nat is a sensible lead-in to the dependent function type α → List α.
Indeed, but that's not the case in type systems of common languages AFAIK

In the Java example, you can easily define an analogous cons function; the signature will look like LinkedList<T> cons(T item, LinkedList<T> list), which in Lean's terms is {T : Type} (item : T) (list : LinkedList T) → LinkedList T. You can't pass the depended-on type in explicitly, but it has to be passed in and so it's done implicitly.

If you really, really want dependence on a number, the Go spec suggests that array types mandatorily depend on a numeric length, and that the length can be specified by a variable, but I'm not familiar enough with Go to know whether the function you outline is indeed possible.

(There's a weird thing going on in Java where array types of particular fixed lengths notionally exist, but you don't declare them as the types of variables. This is far enough removed from the language's type system that I don't want to call it an example. But it's sort of in the area.)

trait Entry { type Key; val key: Key }
def extractKey(e: Entry): e.Key = e.key
val extractor: (e: Entry) => e.Key = extractKey

So the type of extractor is (e: Entry) => e.Key which means e.Key is a type, but since e is a term this demonstrates dependent types: types that depend on terms.

Dependent types mean a type that is parameterized by a value (that may live in another universe than your type).
Some languages allow a subset of it (but they usually don't have the notion of universes and are subject to russell paradox). For example, C++, Rust allow to parameterize a type by a value (like a number).
But this is poors man dependent type.
Usually we refer to dependent type system as a type system that allow a type to be parameterized by the input value of a function, this is where dependent types shine and allow for the definition of ∀. Without this advanced dependent type, you can't define it. This is one of the famous curry howard correspondance items, but an important one.

Here an example definition of ∀ :

-- note P type depends on a value `a ∈ α`
def ForAll {α : Sort u} (P : α → Prop) : Prop := (a: α) → P a
-- with type annotation
notation "∀" a ":" α ", " P => ForAll (fun (a: α) => P)
-- without type annotation (inferred)
notation "∀" a "," P => ForAll (fun a => P)

All of this has nothing to do with functionnal programming (ok, maybe it's roots/origin). it's just type theory.
it just happens a lot of dependent type theory and Curry-Howard correspondance happens to be implemented using functionnal programming. But nothing in theory prevents to build a dependent type system with non functionnal programming languages.
As an example, i built all the curry howard correspondance on top of typescript type system. it's ugly and verbose, but it works given the power of typescript types that are turing complete. And typescript is not a functional programming language.
